sections.title: Food chemistry and energy
sections.text:
Food science connects composition, structure, processing, nutrition, quality and safety. Milk illustrates these connections: lactose, protein and fat supply nutrients, its water supports many reactions and microorganisms, and heat treatment and packaging affect storage. A food's nutrient content alone cannot establish its microbiological safety.

**food.**

Food is a substance consumed to supply energy, nutrients and other components supporting physiological functions. Not everything eaten provides equal nutritional value. Some foods provide substantial energy but relatively few essential micronutrients; others supply high concentrations of vitamins, minerals or fiber. Food science examines four major dimensions:

- **Composition:** What chemicals are present?
- **Structure:** How are these chemicals organized?
- **Transformation:** What happens during cooking, processing, storage and digestion?
- **Safety and quality:** Is the food suitable and safe for consumption?

**nutrients.**

Nutrients are substances the body needs for energy, structure, growth, repair and normal physiological processes. They are conventionally grouped as macronutrients and micronutrients.

**Macronutrients:** Carbohydrates, Proteins, Fats.

**Micronutrients:** Vitamins, Minerals.

Water is an essential nutrient, while dietary fiber is an important carbohydrate component with significant physiological benefits.

**The approximate energy contribution of macronutrients.**

| Nutrient | Approximate metabolizable energy |
|---|---:|
| Carbohydrate | 4 kcal/g |
| Protein | 4 kcal/g |
| Fat | 9 kcal/g |
| Alcohol, although not an essential nutrient | 7 kcal/g |

These are general Atwater energy factors. Actual food-energy calculations can differ with composition, fiber and digestibility.

**Scientific calculation — Food energy.**

Suppose a hypothetical food serving contains:

- 30 g carbohydrate.
- 10 g protein.
- 8 g fat.

Energy from carbohydrate:

$$30\times4=120\text{ kcal}$$

Energy from protein:

$$10\times4=40\text{ kcal}$$

Energy from fat:

$$8\times9=72\text{ kcal}$$

Total estimated energy:

$$\boxed{120+40+72=232\text{ kcal}}$$

**Key relationship:** Fat provides more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate or protein under these general factors.

Energy factors are estimates of metabolizable energy rather than exact combustion values for every food. A kilocalorie is 1000 small calories and equals 4.184 kilojoules. The “Calorie” often used on food labels means a kilocalorie. Water, vitamins and minerals supply essential functions without providing energy through the same oxidation pathways as carbohydrate, protein and fat.

sections.title: Carbohydrates, fibre and starch behaviour
sections.text:
**carbohydrates.**

Carbohydrates are organic compounds that include sugars, starches and dietary fiber. Many have structures containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. They perform several functions in living organisms, including energy supply and structural roles.

**Major carbohydrate categories.**

| Category | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Monosaccharide | Single sugar unit | Glucose, fructose, galactose |
| Disaccharide | Two linked monosaccharide units | Sucrose, lactose, maltose |
| Polysaccharide | Many linked sugar units | Starch, glycogen, cellulose |

**Monosaccharides.**

Glucose is a particularly important metabolic fuel. Fructose occurs naturally in fruits and other foods. Galactose forms part of lactose. These sugars have related but distinct molecular structures and metabolic pathways.

**Disaccharides.**

**Sucrose:** Glucose + fructose.

**Lactose:** Glucose + galactose.

**Maltose:** Two glucose units joined by a glycosidic bond.

Digestive enzymes break these into absorbable monosaccharides.

**Lactose digestion.**

Lactase is an enzyme located at the intestinal brush border. It hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose. If insufficient lactase is present, unabsorbed lactose can draw water into the intestine and undergo fermentation by intestinal microorganisms. This can produce gas, bloating and diarrhea in susceptible individuals. The scientific lesson is that food tolerance depends not only on food composition but also on digestive-enzyme activity.

**Starch.**

Starch is a glucose-storage polysaccharide in plants. Major components include amylose and amylopectin. Sources include wheat, rice, potatoes, maize and many cereals. Digestive amylases hydrolyze accessible starch molecules into smaller carbohydrate products. Other enzymes complete digestion to absorbable sugars.

**Glycogen.**

Glycogen is an extensively branched glucose-storage polymer in animals. The liver stores glycogen that can help maintain blood glucose. Skeletal muscles also store glycogen for local energy metabolism.

**Starch is the major glucose-storage polysaccharide of plants; glycogen is the corresponding major storage polysaccharide in animals.**

**Dietary fiber.**

Dietary fiber consists of carbohydrate components and related substances that resist digestion by human small-intestinal enzymes. It includes forms such as cellulose, some hemicelluloses, pectins and resistant starch. Some dietary fibers are fermented by gut microorganisms, producing short-chain fatty acids. Others contribute substantially to stool bulk or influence intestinal movement.

**Soluble versus insoluble fiber.**

| Soluble fiber | Insoluble fiber |
|---|---|
| Often dissolves or disperses in water | Generally does not dissolve readily |
| Some forms produce viscosity | Often contributes to stool bulk |
| Some forms influence glucose and cholesterol handling | Can support bowel movement |
| Examples: pectin, beta-glucan | Examples: cellulose, some wheat bran |

The categories overlap in their effects. **Fermentability and viscosity** can sometimes be more useful scientific descriptors than solubility alone.

**Why does cooking make starch easier to digest.**

In the presence of sufficient water and heat, starch granules can absorb water and undergo **gelatinization**. Their ordered structure becomes disrupted. Digestive enzymes may then gain easier access to starch molecules. For example, ordinary cooked rice is generally more digestible than uncooked rice. However, cooling some cooked starches can lead to partial retrogradation and increased resistant-starch formation. This demonstrates how food processing changes molecular structure and digestion.

Pectin is a plant-cell-wall polysaccharide that can form gels. Gel formation depends on pectin type, acidity, sugar concentration and, for some formulations, calcium. This explains why making jam involves both composition and controlled processing. A watery mixture with fruit flavour does not necessarily have the same gel structure as a properly formulated preserve.

Gelatinization and gelation are different terms. Gelatinization concerns structural changes in heated starch with water, while gelation describes formation of a network that gives a material gel-like properties. Cooling cooked starch can lead to reassociation called retrogradation, influencing texture and resistant starch. These molecular changes help explain bread staling and changes in cooled rice or potatoes without implying identical effects in every recipe.

sections.title: Proteins, fats and molecular structure
sections.text:
**a protein.**

Proteins are large molecules composed of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. They perform structural, transport, catalytic, immune and regulatory functions. Examples include: Hemoglobin — Oxygen transport. Collagen — Structural support. Amylase — Enzyme. Antibodies — Immune recognition. Actin and myosin — Muscle contraction.

**amino acids.**

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. A typical amino acid contains an amino group, carboxyl group and side chain attached to a central carbon, although their precise structures differ. Human proteins are constructed using twenty standard amino acids. Of these, **nine are essential dietary amino acids for adults**. Essential means the body cannot synthesize enough of them to meet physiological requirements.

**Essential versus nonessential amino acids.**

**Essential:** Must be supplied adequately by the diet.

**Nonessential:** Can be synthesized by the body under normal conditions.

**Conditionally essential:** May need greater dietary supply under particular physiological or pathological conditions.

**The four levels of protein structure.**

| Structural level | process |
|---|---|
| Primary | Amino-acid sequence joined by peptide bonds |
| Secondary | Local structural patterns such as α-helices and β-sheets |
| Tertiary | Three-dimensional folding of a polypeptide |
| Quaternary | Arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits, when present |

Not every protein possesses a quaternary structure.

**protein denaturation.**

Denaturation is a change in a protein's native structure that affects its conformation and often its function. Heat, pH changes and certain chemical conditions can cause denaturation. An everyday example is the coagulation of egg-white proteins during cooking. Heating disrupts the native organization of proteins, exposing regions that can interact and aggregate.

**Important:** Ordinary heat denaturation does not necessarily destroy every peptide bond or convert protein entirely into free amino acids.

**lipids.**

Lipids are a diverse group of molecules with significant hydrophobic characteristics. They include triglycerides, phospholipids, cholesterol and other lipid compounds. Their roles include energy storage, cell-membrane structure, signaling and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

**a triglyceride.**

A triglyceride contains a glycerol backbone connected to three fatty acids through ester bonds. Triglycerides constitute a major form of dietary fat and energy storage.

**Saturated versus unsaturated fats.**

**Saturated fatty acids:** Have no carbon–carbon double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains.

**Monounsaturated fatty acids:** Have one carbon–carbon double bond.

**Polyunsaturated fatty acids:** Have two or more such bonds.

Double-bond configuration influences molecular packing and physical properties.

**Why are many oils liquid.**

Cis double bonds introduce bends into many unsaturated fatty-acid chains. These bends interfere with tight packing of lipid molecules. Consequently, many unsaturated-fat-rich oils are liquid at ordinary room temperatures. However, composition and temperature determine actual physical state, and not every unsaturated fat is liquid under all conditions.

**Trans fats.**

Trans unsaturated fatty acids have a different double-bond geometry from the common cis configuration. Some are produced during industrial processing. High intakes of industrially produced trans fats are associated with adverse cardiovascular effects. WHO recommends limiting trans fat intake to no more than 1% of total energy and avoiding industrially produced trans fats.

**Essential fatty acids.**

Two major essential fatty acids are:

**Linoleic acid:** Omega-6 family.

**Alpha-linolenic acid:** Omega-3 family.

The body cannot make enough of these from other molecules. They must therefore be provided in suitable amounts through food.

Protein quality depends on digestibility and the supply of indispensable amino acids relative to physiological requirements. A limiting amino acid restricts efficient synthesis when other amino acids are available. Combining varied food sources over an adequate diet can improve amino-acid supply; a healthy diet need not rely on one food as a complete solution.

Fat properties depend on chain length, saturation, configuration and mixture composition. Hydrogenation changes unsaturation; partial hydrogenation can create trans configurations. Oxidative rancidity involves reactions of lipids with oxygen, often through radical chain processes. Hydrolytic rancidity releases fatty acids through hydrolysis. Light, oxygen, metals, temperature and packaging can alter deterioration rates. A rancid odour is a quality warning but is not the only possible food hazard.

sections.title: Enzymes, browning and cooking
sections.text:
**Why is water important in food.**

Water is a solvent, reactant and medium for heat and mass transfer. It influences food texture, microbial activity, shelf life and chemical reactions. Milk, fruit and vegetables commonly have relatively high water content. Grains and dried legumes generally contain less water when stored correctly. But two foods with similar total moisture can have very different microbial stability. Water activity, developed in Chapter 24, explains this difference.

**enzymes in food science.**

Enzymes are biological catalysts that accelerate reactions by lowering activation-energy barriers. They are usually proteins, although some catalytic RNA molecules also exist. Food-related examples include: Amylase — Starch breakdown. Proteases — Protein hydrolysis. Lipases — Lipid breakdown. Pectinases — Modification of plant-cell-wall pectin. Polyphenol oxidase — Important in enzymatic browning.

**Why does a cut apple turn brown.**

Cutting damages cells and exposes compounds that were previously separated. Polyphenol oxidase promotes oxidation of suitable phenolic substrates in the presence of oxygen. The resulting reaction products can form brown pigments.

**Enzymatic browning (process):**

```text
Fruit tissue is cut or damaged
    ↓
Enzymes and phenolic substrates gain access to one another
    ↓
Oxygen participates in enzyme-catalyzed oxidation
    ↓
Quinones and related reactive products form
    ↓
Further reactions produce brown-colored materials
```

Lemon juice can slow browning through effects associated with acidity and antioxidant chemistry. Refrigeration can also slow relevant reactions, while controlled blanching can inactivate certain enzymes.

**Browning is not automatically evidence of a foodborne pathogen.**

Enzymatic browning differs from the Maillard reaction. Maillard chemistry involves reducing sugars and amino compounds and contributes to cooked crust colour and flavour. Caramelization involves thermal transformation of sugars. Neither requires polyphenol oxidase in the way cut-apple browning does. Heat treatment may improve digestibility and microbial safety while also reducing some heat-sensitive nutrients; its nutritional effect is therefore not universally harmful or universally beneficial.

questions.prompt: A diet relies almost exclusively on refined cereal protein with an inadequate supply of one essential amino acid. What is the principal nutritional concern?

options.B: The limiting essential amino acid can constrain efficient protein synthesis
options.C: The body no longer requires nitrogen
options.D: Essential amino acids are made freely from minerals

questions.explanation: An essential amino acid supplied in inadequate quantity can limit protein synthesis despite the presence of other amino acids.

questions.prompt: Which fatty acid is a dietary precursor within the omega-3 essential fatty-acid family?
questions.explanation: Alpha-linolenic acid is an essential omega-3 fatty acid that contributes to physiological lipid metabolism.

questions.prompt: Brown pigments form on a heated bread crust through reactions between suitable reducing sugars and amino compounds. This is:
questions.explanation: The Maillard reaction involves reducing sugars and amino groups and contributes to nonenzymatic browning during heating.

questions.prompt: Pectin contributes to the characteristic texture of many jams because it:

options.D: Can form a gel network under suitable acidity, sugar and formulation conditions

questions.explanation: Pectin networks immobilize water and produce a gel, with conditions varying by pectin type and recipe.

questions.prompt: Which deterioration process is especially important in unsaturated-fat-rich foods exposed to oxygen?

options.A: Formation of a new DNA nucleus
options.B: Oxidative rancidity involving lipid oxidation reactions
options.C: Conversion of oil directly to cellulose
options.D: Permanent removal of all free radicals

questions.explanation: Unsaturated lipids can undergo radical-driven oxidation, producing undesirable odors, flavors and chemical products.
